title: useRef — DOM Access, Focus Management, and Mutable Values

subChunks.title: useRef — DOM Access, Focus Management, and Mutable Values
subChunks.hookHtml: useRef serves two distinct purposes that beginners often conflate. First, it gives you a direct reference to a DOM element — letting you focus an input, measure dimensions, or integrate with non-React libraries. Second, it stores a mutable value that persists across renders without causing a re-render when it changes. Both uses are important. Neither replaces state.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
useRef for DOM access

Attach a ref to a JSX element using the ref prop. After render, ref.current points to the DOM node:

import { useRef, useEffect } from 'react';

function SearchModal({ isOpen }) {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (isOpen) inputRef.current?.focus(); // Focus input when modal opens
  }, [isOpen]);

  return <input ref={inputRef} type="text" placeholder="Search..." />;
}

Common DOM ref use cases

  • Auto-focus — focus an input on mount or when a condition changes
  • Measuring dimensions — read ref.current.getBoundingClientRect()
  • Integrating with third-party libs — D3, video players, canvas, maps
  • Triggering imperative animations

useRef for mutable values — the interval ID pattern

Unlike state, ref.current can be mutated directly and the change does not trigger a re-render. This makes it perfect for storing values that the render output doesn't depend on:

function StopwatchWithRef() {
  const [elapsed, setElapsed] = useState(0);
  const intervalRef = useRef(null); // Stores the interval ID — not display data

  function start() {
    intervalRef.current = setInterval(() => {
      setElapsed(e => e + 1);
    }, 1000);
  }

  function stop() {
    clearInterval(intervalRef.current);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <p>{elapsed}s</p>
      <button onClick={start}>Start</button>
      <button onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
    </div>
  );
}

The interval ID belongs in a ref because: (1) it changes over time, (2) the UI doesn't need to re-render when it changes, (3) it needs to persist across renders.

Ref vs state — the decision matrix

QuestionAnswer → Use
Does the UI need to update when this value changes?Yes → State | No → Ref
Does it need to survive re-renders?Yes → Ref or State | No → Local variable
Is it a DOM node?Yes → Ref

Vex: "Refs are escape hatches from React's data flow. Use them for the things React can't manage — DOM manipulation, integration with external libraries, values that tick along without driving the UI. When in doubt, try state first."

Storing previous values

function Counter({ count }) {
  const prevCountRef = useRef();

  useEffect(() => {
    prevCountRef.current = count; // Update AFTER render
  });

  const prevCount = prevCountRef.current;

  return (
    <p>Now: {count} | Before: {prevCount}</p>
  );
}

storyBeats.text: Vex picks up a wand — not for casting spells, but as a pointer. 'Sometimes you need to reach into the DOM directly,' she says. 'Not to change how it looks — React handles that — but to tell it to do something: focus, play, scroll. That's what refs are for.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Two uses. First: a direct handle to a DOM node — for focus, measurement, and third-party integrations. Second: a mutable container for values the render output doesn't depend on. The key difference from state: changing a ref does not trigger a re-render.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <FocusInput /> component:

  • Renders a text <input data-testid="input"> and a <button data-testid="focus-btn">Focus Input</button>
  • Clicking the button programmatically focuses the input using a ref
  • Also render a click counter <p data-testid="clicks"> that tracks how many times the button was clicked — store the interval ID in a ref (not state) as a separate exercise; here just increment a counter in state
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <Stopwatch /> from scratch. Buttons: Start, Stop, Reset. Store the interval ID in a ref (not state). Display elapsed seconds in state (triggers re-renders for display). Stop clears the interval via the ref. Reset clears the interval and sets elapsed to 0.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the two uses of useRef to a colleague who only knows useState. When would you use a ref instead of state? Give a concrete example where putting a value in state instead of a ref would cause a bug or unnecessary re-renders.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between useRef and useState?
options: Mutating a ref does not trigger a re-render; updating state always does
Refs persist across renders; state is reset on every render
Refs can only hold DOM elements; state can hold any value
useState is for primitives; useRef is for objects and arrays
questions.answer: Mutating a ref does not trigger a re-render; updating state always does
questions.explanation: Both refs and state persist across renders. The critical difference: calling a state setter schedules a re-render; mutating ref.current does not. Use state for values that drive the UI; use refs for values the render output doesn't depend on.

questions.prompt: A modal should auto-focus its first input when it opens. Which approach is correct?
options: Attach a ref to the input; in a useEffect that watches the isOpen prop, call ref.current.focus()
Use document.querySelector inside the modal component's render function
Set autoFocus={true} on the input (always focuses, even when modal is closed)
Pass a callback prop from the parent that imperatively focuses the input
questions.answer: Attach a ref to the input; in a useEffect that watches the isOpen prop, call ref.current.focus()
questions.explanation: The ref gives you a direct DOM handle. The useEffect fires after render when isOpen changes to true — the DOM element exists by then so focus() works. document.querySelector breaks React's encapsulation. autoFocus only fires on initial mount.

questions.prompt: A setInterval ID needs to be stored so it can be cleared by a Stop button. Should it be stored in state or a ref?
options: A ref — the interval ID doesn't affect the UI and doesn't need to trigger a re-render
State — all values that change over time should be stored in state
A local variable — it only needs to persist for the duration of the interval
A constant defined outside the component
questions.answer: A ref — the interval ID doesn't affect the UI and doesn't need to trigger a re-render
questions.explanation: The interval ID is needed for clearInterval but has no effect on what's displayed. Putting it in state would trigger an unnecessary re-render when Start is clicked. A local variable wouldn't survive across renders (it's re-created each render). A ref persists across renders without causing re-renders.
